findings.title: WHO/UNICEF Joint Monitoring Programme — drinking water service levels
findings.summary: Bundled demo source (no live search was run) — The JMP tracks Ghana's drinking-water service levels and the regional differences within them. Northern Ghana is routinely treated as a distinct planning context from the coastal south, with a larger share of the population dependent on point sources rather than piped supply.

findings.title: BGS Africa Groundwater Atlas — Ghana hydrogeology
findings.summary: Bundled demo source (no live search was run) — The BGS Africa Groundwater Atlas describes northern Ghana as largely underlain by the Voltaian sedimentary basin, where groundwater occurs mainly in fractures rather than in a continuous porous aquifer. Borehole yields in this setting are typically low and highly variable, and drilling failure rates are higher than in weathered-basement terrain.

findings.title: WaterAid — Ghana country programme
findings.summary: Bundled demo source (no live search was run) — WaterAid runs a country programme in Ghana with a long-standing focus on underserved communities in the northern regions. Its programme framing identifies rural and peri-urban northern communities as priority areas for water-point provision and rehabilitation.

findings.title: World Bank — Water global practice
findings.summary: Bundled demo source (no live search was run) — The World Bank supports water-supply and sanitation investment in Ghana, including small-town and rural service delivery. Tamale is a well-connected regional capital on the national trunk road network, which generally eases equipment mobilisation relative to remote districts.

findings.title: FAO AQUASTAT — water resources information
findings.summary: Bundled demo source (no live search was run) — AQUASTAT compiles national water-resource and rainfall-seasonality data. Northern Ghana has a single pronounced wet season followed by a long dry season, so storage sizing and dry-season yield are the binding constraints on any surface- or shallow-source scheme.
findings.sourceName: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations

findings.title: IRC — water services in Ghana and life-cycle costs
findings.summary: Bundled demo source (no live search was run) — IRC has a long-running Ghana programme focused on making water services last, using life-cycle cost analysis that counts operation and maintenance alongside construction. That framing consistently shows recurrent costs as the decisive factor in whether a rural water point stays functional.

population.methodLabel: 950,124 reported residents of Tamale (2010), OpenStreetMap, split by this site's share of mapped buildings (181 of 4,000 in the analysis area).
limitations: The published population figure covers the whole of Tamale, Tamale Metropolitan District, Northern Region, NT-0148-3057, Ghana; distributing it by building count assumes household size is uniform across the settlement.
OpenStreetMap building coverage is uneven, so a well-mapped neighbourhood is credited with a larger share than a poorly mapped one of the same size.
Neighbour counts are measured within 400 m of the site and scaled by area to the 1000 m service radius; real settlement is not uniform.
Everyone inside the service radius is assumed to be able and willing to walk to the point; terrain, land tenure and social barriers are not modelled.

recommendation.label: Roof rainwater harvesting with seasonal storage
rationale: Groundwater evidence score is 0.26, below the 0.35 threshold — drilling here is a poor bet.
Annual rainfall is 1,074 mm, at or above the 700 mm that makes roof harvesting worth the catchment investment.
With 4 months below 30 mm, storage rather than yield is the binding constraint on this option.

components.name: Roof catchment
components.detail: 1,500 m2 of guttered institutional roof with first-flush diverters and leaf screens.

components.name: Storage
components.detail: 150,000 L of storage, sized at 100 L per m2 of catchment to bridge the 4-month dry season.

components.name: Distribution
components.detail: 688 m of conceptual distribution pipeline feeding 1 tap stand(s).

components.name: Monitoring
components.detail: Flow and system-status sensors with remote reporting for post-handover verification.

cost.accessMultiplierReason: Site is 35 m from the nearest mapped road on flat terrain — 1% mobilisation and logistics surcharge applied.
assumptions: Order-of-magnitude planning ranges for pre-feasibility screening — not a quotation, tender price or bill of quantities.
Quantities are sized for approximately 176 people at the service level assumed by the upstream sizing step.
Access surcharge applied to the subtotal: x1.01. Site is 35 m from the nearest mapped road on flat terrain — 1% mobilisation and logistics surcharge applied.
Totals are rounded outward to the nearest $1,000 (low down, high up) to avoid implying precision the method does not have.
Excludes land acquisition, taxes and import duties, permitting fees, contingency, and all recurrent operation and maintenance costs.
All unit rates are taken unchanged from the project coefficient table (RWSN/UNICEF rural water supply cost benchmarking (planning range)).
Catchment area is derived from storage at 100 L of tank per m2 of roof, matching the upstream sizing rule; it assumes existing institutional roofs are available for retrofit.

output.formula: 1,500 m2 x (1,074 mm / 1,000) x runoff coefficient 0.8 x 1,000 / 365 days = 3,530 L/day gross; low bound applies operational efficiency 0.82 = 2,890-3,530 L/day
caveats: Desk-study planning figures only. Borehole yield in particular is not guaranteed by a desk study: the sustainable rate must be confirmed by a step-drawdown and constant-rate pumping test on the completed borehole.
People supported assumes 20 L/person/day (WHO/UNICEF JMP service-level guidance); real consumption varies with walking distance, queueing time and the alternatives available.
No allowance is made for livestock, irrigation, institutional or commercial demand, which routinely consume a large share of a rural water point's output.
This is an annual average. Rainwater supply is strongly seasonal: in the dry months the system delivers nothing and the community depends entirely on stored volume.
Assumes the full roof area is guttered, in good condition, and made of a material suitable for potable collection.
Gravity-fed system with no pump, so there is no pump rate to report.

recommendation.coverageNote: An estimated 30,095-55,891 people live within the 1,000 m service radius, but one installation of this type can supply 144-176. The system is sized to its own sustainable yield; covering the full catchment would require multiple installations.
assumptions: Residents within the service radius: 950,124 reported residents of Tamale (2010), OpenStreetMap, split by this site's share of mapped buildings (181 of 4,000 in the analysis area). (range 30,095-55,891).

An estimated 30,095-55,891 people live within the 1,000 m service radius, but one installation of this type can supply 144-176. The system is sized to its own sustainable yield; covering the full catchment would require multiple installations.

The published population figure covers the whole of Tamale, Tamale Metropolitan District, Northern Region, NT-0148-3057, Ghana; distributing it by building count assumes household size is uniform across the settlement.
OpenStreetMap building coverage is uneven, so a well-mapped neighbourhood is credited with a larger share than a poorly mapped one of the same size.
Neighbour counts are measured within 400 m of the site and scaled by area to the 1000 m service radius; real settlement is not uniform.
Everyone inside the service radius is assumed to be able and willing to walk to the point; terrain, land tenure and social barriers are not modelled.
Demand is taken as 20 L/person/day (WHO/UNICEF JMP service-level guidance).
Catchment is capped at 1500 m2 of available roof, so this option supports 144-176 people.
Pipeline length (688 m) and tap-stand count (1) are a conceptual layout from the geospatial step, not a surveyed route.
Order-of-magnitude planning ranges for pre-feasibility screening — not a quotation, tender price or bill of quantities.
Quantities are sized for approximately 176 people at the service level assumed by the upstream sizing step.
Access surcharge applied to the subtotal: x1.01. Site is 35 m from the nearest mapped road on flat terrain — 1% mobilisation and logistics surcharge applied.
Totals are rounded outward to the nearest $1,000 (low down, high up) to avoid implying precision the method does not have.
Excludes land acquisition, taxes and import duties, permitting fees, contingency, and all recurrent operation and maintenance costs.
All unit rates are taken unchanged from the project coefficient table (RWSN/UNICEF rural water supply cost benchmarking (planning range)).
Catchment area is derived from storage at 100 L of tank per m2 of roof, matching the upstream sizing rule; it assumes existing institutional roofs are available for retrofit.
requiredValidation: Hydrogeological review and ground geophysical survey (resistivity or TEM) at the shortlisted point before any commitment.
Water-quality testing against national and WHO standards, including bacteriological, fluoride, arsenic, nitrate and salinity.
Land ownership confirmation and legal right of access or easement for the site and the pipeline corridor.
Community consultation on siting, tariff, and the operation and maintenance model, including who holds the spares.
Seasonal access verification — confirm the approach is passable for rigs and delivery vehicles in the wet season.
Environmental and social review, including abstraction licensing and downstream or aquifer impact.
Final engineering design, bill of quantities and competitive tender.

narrative: Roof rainwater harvesting in Tamale can supply 144 to 176 people daily with 2,890 to 3,530 liters, serving 42,993 within the service radius. Costs range from $121,000 to $240,000; groundwater is unsuitable, and storage limits output. These are pre-feasibility estimates requiring field validation.
